eyebrow: CureGRIN · GRIN2B Conference, Bethesda · 18 Jul 2026 · Researcher long-form
title: Dr. Andrew Penn:
headline: At this meeting, scientists stop showing off and start asking each other for help, because the families matter more.
story: Dr. Penn opens on an honest line: “we're not sure why it's not working, but we're really looking for help.” Then his work in plain words, how this meeting works (scientists share unfinished work, families say what matters), and why it feels different: no childlike competition, a united front.

This is the only researcher film about how scientists behave with each other. Do not tell the other three stories here (Traynelis = why research is slow, Roche = NIH, Park = the clinic). Keep the science short. It must feel hopeful and human: patient work, done together.
do: Open on him/her speaking, mid-answer, with the hook text. Nothing else on frame 1.
Name plate on the first on-camera line after the hook, small, lower left, never before 0:03.
Captions from the first word to the last. Type CureGRIN, GRIN2B, GRIN, NMDA, NIH correctly.
Cut between sentences. Quotes stay as spoken.
Frame tighter than the camera did: the 4K source gives you room.
dont: No logo, name plate or fade at 0:00.
Never say or show that GRIN disorders can be prevented, are anyone's fault, or have a cure soon.
No shots of people eating. No childcare-room shots unless Nick confirms consent.
Do not reuse a B-roll shot that another researcher film uses.

[00:47] Yeah, I'm Dr. Andrew Penn. I'm an assistant professor at the University of Sussex in England
[00:52] near Brighton, and I work on NMDA receptors. NMDA receptors are encoded by Grin genes,
[01:00] and Grin genes are, some people have genetic changes in Grin genes, and that can lead to
[01:08] neurodevelopmental disorders or neurological disorders, and so I have an interest in trying
[01:15] to understand what those variants are doing and how we can actually go about understanding
[01:23] the way the receptors change at synapses, the connections between neurons and the brain,
[01:27] potentially how we could actually develop therapies in the future to treating those
[01:33] patients, yeah. So why does it matter for science and family to come together in person
[01:40] at an event like this? So I really like the format of this type of conference. So the
[01:46] way that they have both sort of researcher-only section and sort of family-only section and
[01:52] then a sort of researcher and family joint session, I think for me the benefit of having
[01:58] both parts, both first with the researcher-only section, it means that we can really open
[02:03] up to other researchers in the detail of the sort of research findings that we're making.
[02:10] We obviously talk about a lot of unpublished work, ongoing work, and it's really a good
[02:15] opportunity to get input from other researchers on potentially also for new collaborations.
[02:23] So that's been really helpful. We wouldn't get that if we only had family-oriented presentations
[02:27] because we just wouldn't get the detail. But with the family-based talks, this is an
[02:33] opportunity for us to communicate to families about the sort of work we're doing and the
[02:39] sort of potential benefits that that could have down the line. So I think that's a really
[02:44] powerful thing. It's also a chance for us to hear from families themselves about the
[02:52] challenges that they face, what they consider priorities, and that ultimately can feed into
[02:59] not only motivating the sort of research that we're doing, motivating us to apply for more
[03:06] grants, do more research into it, but also it motivates us to orientate our research
[03:12] direction to actually benefit those patients or the families. So, you know, us all coming
[03:18] together is a really powerful thing. And every time I do one of these, come to one of these
[03:23] conferences, I feel a great benefit from it.
[03:28] Interviewer: What do you hope families better understand about the progress being made?
[03:34] So I think it's difficult for people outside of research or science to appreciate the extent
[03:44] the time that it takes and the kind of time and effort it takes to make progress. And
[03:53] I think it's important for them to understand that. And it's not like one of those things
[03:58] where if you work harder, you'll always get results, because you work harder, but that
[04:05] just helps you to find out whether or not something has worked. And if it hasn't worked,
[04:11] then we have to, it can take then a lot longer. The path is very convoluted, but you just
[04:16] hope that eventually you can get to where you want to go with this and ultimately have
[04:23] the benefit.
[05:01] Interviewer: So why are the conferences like this important for future research and collaboration?
[05:05] Yeah, so I think I touched on this in a previous answer to a previous question. I think that
[05:12] that's where I think the researcher talks come into play. Having said that, actually
[05:18] in the family talks, we have to make things really accessible. And sometimes even the
[05:23] researchers struggle to follow the main narrative of a researcher talk, especially if it's
[05:30] a slightly different field. So what it is is a nice opportunity in those family talks
[05:35] when other researchers are present, is that they capture the essence properly of what
[05:40] you're doing. And actually it helps them to sort of realise, especially if they are
[05:44] in a different field, that they could contribute or could suggest a way forward that actually
[05:51] might help the research in a way that we didn't anticipate ourselves, because we all
[05:55] have different experiences and different expertise, and ultimately that can help us in different
[06:01] ways. And with the researcher talks, if we are, when researchers are talking to each
[06:06] other in sort of the more, in the details, this is an opportunity that when people are
[06:11] facing more challenges at a detailed level, that we can really thrash out ideas about
[06:19] what is going on. And I think this meeting in particular has been a good example of that
[06:24] for me. It's not so much been a display, like a display of our beautiful research findings,
[06:33] it's been more of a sort of laying out what we've got on the table and going, ah, we've
[06:38] got this working, this working, this, we're not sure why it's not working, but we're really
[06:43] looking for help and ideas and let's discuss ways forward with it. And that's what this
[06:49] meeting's been about for me and it's been really helpful.
[06:53] Interviewer: For someone considering attending next year, what would you say is invaluable?
[07:02] As a researcher, or, yeah, I think as a researcher, so in different, so something that's really
[07:10] unique about these type of conferences and working together with parent-led organisations
[07:18] like this, is that there is more a united front. I mean, I remember going to sort of
[07:28] some discovery science type events or conferences and it's almost like there's this childlike
[07:38] competition and argument almost about a particular finding, especially when there are two groups
[07:47] who are getting different results looking at the same thing. And rather than sort of
[07:52] coming together and then trying to work out it together and then come up with a unanimous
[08:00] outcome, they just, it's just like a little cat and mouse and just trying to, yeah, so
[08:09] it's much more collaborative is what I'm trying to say. And I think that is, it feels nicer
[08:16] and it feels like it should, yeah, it feels like how science should. I think part of
[08:21] the reason why it's like that is because if it was like some of those other meetings
[08:27] that I was talking about, it wouldn't look good to people. It's like, this is what science
[08:33] is like. And actually, I think, you know, when we look at ourselves and go, actually,
[08:40] it shouldn't be like that. And I think having, taking the squabbles out of it and thinking,
[08:47] well, this, you know, these kids have got something that's, and these families are going
[08:50] through something that's much more important than what we're squabbling about. Yeah. So
[08:54] I think that's what comes from this and why I always, yeah, I think that researchers considering
[09:00] it should go for it because it's much more rewarding, it's much more pleasant and it's,
[09:06] you can get a lot more out of it in terms of collaboration, I think.
